subject: africanElephant
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: adult African bush elephant.
Style: low-poly.
reasoning:
I'm planning a realistically-scaled elephant model at actual size, around 3.2m shoulder height, and starting to lay out the skeleton hierarchy with hip, spine, chest, and neck joints.

I'm working out the spine path coordinates and body sweep radius so the back and belly heights match a real elephant's proportions, adjusting the axis and radii values to get believable body width and depth before moving on to the neck and limb chains.

Continuing from the body, I'm placing the head joint and sizing it as a dome-shaped sphere, then plotting the trunk's curve with catmull points running from the head base down to the ground and curling slightly upward at the tip, setting up the trunk as a chain of segments parented to the head.

Now I'm defining the legs as near-vertical pillar chains with hip, knee, and foot points for each side, keeping elephant legs mostly straight columns, and adding ring-like wrinkle stripes along the trunk using a sine-based pattern.

Foot disk sits as a flat cylinder at the ankle. Legs parent to the hips or spine joints depending on hind/front placement, and I'm now setting up the neck chain parented to the spine's last joint, connecting toward where the head will attach.

I'll simplify by giving the head its own joint instead of expanding the neck chain into multiple names, positioning it with a direction facing forward. For the head itself, I'm layering spheres -- a main skull shape plus a smaller forehead sphere -- scaled and offset slightly to build up the shape.

Now I'm working out the ears: extruded African-style ear shapes attached to head joints on each side, with an outline traced through several points to get the characteristic curved silhouette, then extruded with a slight outward flare and thickness.

For eyes, I'm placing small dark spheres on the skull surface using angle-based positioning around the head center, with a thin lighter rim detail for realism.

Now I'm working out the jaw as a scaled box near the mouth, with the trunk covering most of it below the joint, and planning the tusks as a curved spline path sweeping down and forward from a base point near the mouth.

Tapering the tail into a sweep down from hips to a tip, then adding a tuft of small bristle spikes radiating outward at the end to give it texture.

For the body I'm varying the sweep radius along the path to get a rounded, slightly heavier midsection with a lower belly offset, plus adding bumps for shoulders and head. Then I'm layering the skin paint: a mottled gray base with brownish dust accumulating on the lower body and some wrinkle detailing blended in.

Adding noise-based wrinkle blotches with top lightening, ring patterns on the trunk using sine thresholds, small spike shapes at the trunk tip, and toenail boxes for each foot.

For the ears I'm shading the inner surface with a pinkish tint blended into the base skin tone using a smoothstep-based blotch for vein-like detail, then defining joint bones for the left ear anchored to the head.

Now I'm setting up the trunk and body skeleton: giving each chain a role (tentacle for trunk, spine, tail, hinge for ears, leg joints named hip/knee/ankle per leg), then sweeping a tapered cylindrical shape along the trunk's path with a skin-colored ring pattern applied through the paint function.

I'm placing the head geometry precisely — positioning the skull sphere, aligning the trunk's starting point at the forehead so it emerges naturally, adding twin forehead domes, and checking how the head joins the body so the proportions read correctly before placing the eyes by coordinate.

Good, the eyelid sits slightly embedded as expected. Now working out the jaw placement with a flattened sphere near the trunk base, then thinking about shoulder bumps and spine ridge details before positioning the front leg hip joint within the body's radius at that height.

Setting up the leg kinematics now, computing root-to-target distances to determine knee bend direction for front and hind legs, then sweeping the leg geometry with a tapered radius profile along the chain.

Now I'm adding the foot cylinders positioned at each leg tip with a slight taper, checking overall body height dimensions come out reasonable, and confirming the color palette and paint materials are sufficiently varied across the model.

Setting up the hips joint and spine chain, then sweeping the body profile along it with an interpolated radius function to shape the torso.
